claims.claim: The frontals of †Brachydegma are longer than wide.
claims.source: The frontals are longer than wide, with their posteroventral margin bearing an indentation for the insertion of the dermopterotics.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The parietals of †Brachydegma are quadrangular.
claims.source: The parietals are quadrangular, and the midline suture between the bilateral counterparts of the frontals and parietals anastomoses.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: Each parietal of †Brachydegma bears a lateral extension that inserts into the body of the adjacent dermopterotic.
claims.source: Each parietal bears a lateral extension that inserts into the body of the adjacent dermopterotic.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: There is no independent accessory parietal in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: There is no independent accessory parietal as suggested by Dunkle, 1939.
claims.evidence: This is a reinterpretation of previous descriptions based on new observations.

claims.claim: The dermopterotics of †Brachydegma are longer than wide.
claims.source: The dermopterotics are longer than wide.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The anterior and posterior portions of the dermopterotic of †Brachydegma are connected by a ventral bridge of bone and constitute a single ossification.
claims.source: On the right side of the skull, the anterior and posterior portions of the dermopterotic are clearly connected by a ventral bridge of bone and unambiguously constitute a single ossification, in contrast to the separate intertemporal and supratemporal of many Devonian and some Carboniferous actinopterygians (Gardiner, 1984; Gardiner and Schaeffer, 1989).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens, contrasted with the condition in other taxa.

claims.claim: †Brachydegma has a pair of lateromedially elongate lateral extrascapulars posterior to the parietals.
claims.source: A pair of lateromedially elongate lateral extrascapulars lie posterior to the parietals.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The dermosphenotic of †Brachydegma is sub-rectangular, with a posterior ramus.
claims.source: The canal-bearing dermosphenotic (postorbital in Dunkle, 1939, and Hurley et al., 2007) is sub-rectangular, with a posterior ramus.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: Three infraorbitals surround the posterior and ventral margins of the orbit in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: Three infraorbitals (named here as infraorbital, jugal, lachrymal) surround the posterior and ventral margins of the orbit, with the lachrymal bearing a possible anterior thickening.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The preopercle of †Brachydegma is taller than wide, and sits almost upright in the cheek.
claims.source: The preopercle is taller than wide, and sits almost upright in the cheek.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The preopercle of †Brachydegma bears an overlap area for the maxilla.
claims.source: It bears an overlap area for the maxilla, shown clearly on the right side of the skull where the two bones have pulled away from each other.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: Three additional dorsoventrally arranged anamestic bones separate the preopercle from the opercular series in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: Three additional dorsoventrally arranged anamestic bones separate the preopercle from the opercular series, on the right side of the type specimen (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens, with reference to Figure 2.

claims.claim: The dorsal-most of the three anamestic bones between the preopercle and opercular series in †Brachydegma constitutes the unfused dermohyal.
claims.source: The dorsal-most constitutes the unfused dermohyal, and the ventral two represent accessory opercles.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on position and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The ventral two of the three anamestic bones between the preopercle and opercular series in †Brachydegma represent accessory opercles.
claims.source: The dorsal-most constitutes the unfused dermohyal, and the ventral two represent accessory opercles.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on position and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The accessory opercles of †Brachydegma are broadly comparable to those of the †acrolepidids sensu lato.
claims.source: The latter are broadly comparable to those of the †acrolepidids sensu lato (Aldinger, 1937; Nielsen, 1942).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with other taxa, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The opercle of †Brachydegma is rhomboidal and is of almost equal size to the more quadrate subopercle.
claims.source: The opercle is rhomboidal and is of almost equal size to the more quadrate subopercle.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: At least eight branchiostegal rays are present in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: At least eight branchiostegal rays are present.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The two lateral gulars of †Brachydegma are rostrocaudally elongate and underlie the posterior half of the lower jaw.
claims.source: The two lateral gulars are rostrocaudally elongate and underlie the posterior half of the lower jaw.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The median gular of †Brachydegma is longer than wide, and of subequal length to the lateral gulars.
claims.source: The median gular is longer than wide, and of subequal length to the lateral gulars.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The posttemporal of †Brachydegma is subquadrate and seems to form an anterolateral ramus.
claims.source: The posttemporal is subquadrate and seems to form an anterolateral ramus, likely excluding the extrascapular from the lateral margin of the skull roof.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The supracleithrum of †Brachydegma is ovoidal and larger than the posttemporal.
claims.source: The supracleithrum is ovoidal and larger than the posttemporal, reaches further posteriorly than the cleithrum, and forms a strongly convex and serrated posterior margin.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The postcleithra of †Brachydegma appear to have been three to four in number.
claims.source: The postcleithra are poorly preserved, but appear to have been three to four in number.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens, with some uncertainty due to preservation.

claims.claim: Fringing fulcra line the anterior margin of the pectoral fin in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: Fringing fulcra line the anterior margin of the pectoral fin.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens.

claims.claim: The braincase of †Brachydegma comprises several ossifications, with large gaps presumably filled by cartilage in life.
claims.source: The braincase comprises several ossifications, with large gaps presumably filled by cartilage in life.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and inference about unossified regions.

claims.claim: Three distinct ossifications contribute to the occipital region of †Brachydegma: a basioccipital and a pair of exoccipitals.
claims.source: Three distinct ossifications contribute to the occipital region (boc, exo, Figure 5): a basioccipital and a pair of exoccipitals, comparable to neopterygians (Patterson, 1975; Grande and Bemis, 1998; Grande, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with neopterygians.

claims.claim: The occipital ossifications of †Brachydegma are comparable to neopterygians.

claims.evidence: This is a comparison with neopterygians, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The basioccipital of †Brachydegma projects posteriorly and encloses a short endoskeletal aortic canal.
claims.source: The basioccipital projects posteriorly and encloses a short endoskeletal aortic canal.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The exoccipitals of †Brachydegma form the dorsal margin of the notochordal opening and surround the foramen magnum.

claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.source: Unlike in many crown neopterygians (Patterson, 1975; Grande and Bemis, 1998; Grande, 2010), the exoccipitals do not enclose the vagus nerve.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with crown neopterygians.

claims.claim: The sphenoid ossification of †Brachydegma exhibits a deep, paired posterior myodome.

claims.source: The lateral dorsal aortae of †Brachydegma exit the basicranium and extend along the ventral surface of the parasphenoid, divided by a median keel.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The ascending processes of the parasphenoid of †Brachydegma are well developed and bear a spiracular groove.
claims.source: The posterodorsally directed ascending processes are well developed and bear a spiracular groove.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: A dermal basipterygoid process is absent in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: A dermal basipterygoid process is absent.

claims.source: The dermal and endoskeletal palate of †Brachydegma (Figure 6A–E, H and J) is deep along most of its length, with a convex, imperforate dorsal margin.

claims.claim: A long and broad accessory vomer lies along the medial surface of the anterior half of the palate in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: A long and broad accessory vomer lies along the medial surface of the anterior half of the palate.

claims.source: The quadrate is located posteroventrally and bears two small articular condyles and a gentle posterior groove.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: A dorsolateral flange on the palate of †Brachydegma is the only trace of the metapterygoid.
claims.source: A dorsolateral flange on the palate, slightly anterior to the level of the jaw articulation, is the only trace of the metapterygoid, and seems to resemble the metapterygoid process of neopterygians (Olsen, 1984; Arratia and Schultze, 1991).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with neopterygians.

claims.claim: An autopalatine has not been located in either specimen of †Brachydegma and was probably not mineralized in life.
claims.source: An autopalatine has not been located in either specimen and was probably not mineralized in life.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and inference about unossified structures.

claims.claim: An ossified labial element is present near the ventral opening of the mandibular adductor chamber in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: An ossified labial element is present near the ventral opening of the mandibular adductor chamber, in both sides of the type specimen (calg, lbe, Figure 6A, F and G).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The ossified labial element of †Brachydegma is approximately tear-shaped and perforated.
claims.source: The one of the right side is more completely preserved, and is approximately tear-shaped and perforated, resembling the ones found in, for example, †Boreosomus reuterskioldi and †Ptycholepis bollensis (Véran, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The hyomandibula of †Brachydegma forms rather broad and distinct dorsal and ventral limbs, is perforate, and appears to bear a short and broad opercular process.
claims.source: The hyomandibula (Figure 7A–D) forms rather broad and distinct dorsal and ventral limbs, is perforate, and appears to bear a short and broad opercular process.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: An unfused dermohyal sits on the lateral surface of the dorsal limb of the hyomandibula in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: An unfused dermohyal sits on the lateral surface of the dorsal limb of the hyomandibula.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: Two accessory hyoid elements are preserved in close association with the ventral tip of the hyomandibula on the left side of the holotype of †Brachydegma.
claims.source: On the left side of the holotype, two accessory hyoid elements are preserved, in close association with the ventral tip of the hyomandibula (ih, sy, Figure 8A–E), and are aligned sub-parallel to one another.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The anterior accessory hyoid ossification of †Brachydegma is identified as a symplectic.
claims.source: We identify the anterior ossification as a symplectic and the posterior ossification as an interhyal based on their position, morphology, and relationship with other ossifications (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The posterior accessory hyoid ossification of †Brachydegma is identified as an interhyal.
claims.source: We identify the anterior ossification as a symplectic and the posterior ossification as an interhyal based on their position, morphology, and relationship with other ossifications (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The symplectic of †Brachydegma is subquadrangular, and articulates with the anteroventral tip of the hyomandibula.
claims.source: The symplectic is subquadrangular, and articulates with the anteroventral tip of the hyomandibula (syf, Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The anterior surface of the symplectic of †Brachydegma forms a keel, which likely fit in a groove on the posterior surface of the quadrate.
claims.source: Its anterior surface forms a keel, which likely fit in a groove on the posterior surface of the quadrate (qdgr, Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and inference about articulation.

claims.claim: The anteroventral tip of the symplectic of †Brachydegma forms a thickening, or condyle, which inserts in a facet on the posterior surface of the articular.
claims.source: The anteroventral tip of the symplectic forms a thickening, or condyle, which inserts in a facet on the posterior surface of the articular; its posteroventral tip is produced as a thin, ventrally directed process, which contacts the posterior surface of the articular (cnd, vpsy?, Figure 8C–E).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: A faint groove on the anterodorsal face of the symplectic of †Brachydegma is likely for the passage of the afferent mandibular artery.
claims.source: A faint groove on the anterodorsal face is likely for the passage of the afferent mandibular artery (afmd, Figure 8C–E).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and inference about function.

claims.claim: A similar groove to that on the symplectic of †Brachydegma is present in some †parasemionotids.
claims.source: A similar groove is present in some †parasemionotids (NHMD 74424A; Figure 8F–I), and the putative symplectic of †Pteronisculus (Figure 8J–M).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data from comparative specimens.

claims.claim: The interhyal of †Brachydegma is rod-shaped, and articulates with the posteroventral tip of the hyomandibula.
claims.source: The more posterior of the two elements present in †Brachydegma, identified as an interhyal, is rod-shaped, and articulates with the posteroventral tip of the hyomandibula.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The contact between the symplectic and articular in †Brachydegma forms a double jaw joint.
claims.source: The contact between the symplectic and articular – a double jaw joint – as well as the sub-parallel arrangement of the symplectic and the interhyal resemble that of crown neopterygians, such as †parasemionotids (Stensiö, 1932; Patterson, 1973; Olsen, 1984; Figure 8F–I), †Parapholidophorus (Arratia, 2013), as well as †pycnodonts (Nursall and Maisey, 1987; Gardiner et al., 1996; Kriwet, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The sub-parallel arrangement of the symplectic and the interhyal in †Brachydegma resembles that of crown neopterygians.
claims.source: The contact between the symplectic and articular – a double jaw joint – as well as the sub-parallel arrangement of the symplectic and the interhyal resemble that of crown neopterygians, such as †parasemionotids (Stensiö, 1932; Patterson, 1973; Olsen, 1984; Figure 8F–I), †Parapholidophorus (Arratia, 2013), as well as †pycnodonts (Nursall and Maisey, 1987; Gardiner et al., 1996; Kriwet, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: A single, laterally grooved, plate-like ceratohyal is ossified on each side of the hyoid arch of †Brachydegma.
claims.source: A single, laterally grooved, plate-like ceratohyal is ossified on each side of the hyoid arch of †Brachydegma (Figures 7B, E, 9A, B).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The branchial skeleton of the type specimen of †Brachydegma is nearly complete.
claims.source: The branchial skeleton of the type specimen is nearly complete (Figure 9), although the pharyngobranchials are somewhat disarticulated and shifted from their life positions.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The branchial skeleton of †Brachydegma exhibits the common motif of five ossified branchial arches.
claims.source: The branchial skeleton of †Brachydegma exhibits the common motif of five ossified branchial arches.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: One or two basibranchials are preserved in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: One or two basibranchials are preserved (bb/bh?, bb, Figure 9C, E).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data, with some uncertainty.

claims.claim: Five ceratobranchials are present in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: Five ceratobranchials are present (cb1–5, Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The first four ceratobranchials of †Brachydegma are curved.
claims.source: The first four ceratobranchials are curved.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The fifth ceratobranchial of †Brachydegma is reduced to a tiny rod-like structure.
claims.source: The fifth ceratobranchial is reduced to a tiny rod-like structure.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The first three epibranchials of †Brachydegma bear uncinate processes.
claims.source: The first three epibranchials (ep1–3, Figure 9) bear uncinate processes, with the first two being particularly well developed, like in, for example, †Australosomus (Nielsen, 1949).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The fourth epibranchial of †Brachydegma is short and wide and forms a long and thin anterior process.
claims.source: The fourth epibranchial is short and wide and forms a long and thin anterior process, and a laterally expanded plate supporting the passage of the efferent branchial artery.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: No expanded toothplates are associated with the epibranchials of †Brachydegma.
claims.source: No expanded toothplates are associated with the epibranchials.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The first infrapharyngobranchial of †Brachydegma is rod-shaped and edentulous.
claims.source: The first infrapharyngobranchial is rod-shaped and edentulous.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The second infrapharyngobranchial of †Brachydegma is wider and plate-like, and bears putative teeth on its ventral surface.
claims.source: The second infrapharyngobranchial is wider and plate-like, and bears putative teeth on its ventral surface.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The maxilla of †Brachydegma exhibits a robust horizontal process which supports a single series of large, pointed teeth.
claims.source: The maxilla exhibits a robust horizontal process (Figure 6J), which supports a single series of large, pointed teeth.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and direct observation.

claims.claim: The posterior plate of the maxilla of †Brachydegma is well developed, flat, and tall.
claims.source: The posterior plate of the maxilla is well developed, flat, and tall, with its posterodorsal margin fitting in a notch on the preopercle.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and direct observation.

claims.claim: The maxilla of †Brachydegma forms a well-developed horizontal lamina for attachment to the dermal palate.
claims.source: Medially, the maxilla forms a well-developed horizontal lamina for attachment to the dermal palate (mxhl, Figure 6C–E and J), similar to that of stem actinopterygians like †Mimipiscis, †Pteronisculus, or †Australosomus (Nielsen, 1942; Nielsen, 1949; Gardiner, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The maxilla of MCZ VPF-6504 does not possess a posterior notch.
claims.source: The maxilla of MCZ VPF-6504 does not possess a posterior notch, contrasting a previous reconstruction of this feature (Hurley et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and contrasts with previous interpretations.

claims.claim: There is no evidence for a rod-like articular process with the ethmoid region of the skull in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: We do not find evidence for a rod-like articular process with the ethmoid region of the skull like that of neopterygians (see, for example, Amia in Grande and Bemis, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with neopterygians.

claims.claim: The maxilla of †Brachydegma has a short and thin, plate-like anterior process for firm articulation with the ethmoid and dermal snout ossifications of the skull.

claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The dentary of †Brachydegma is the principal bone of the lateral surface of the jaw, and bears a single row of teeth.
claims.source: The dentary (dnt, Figures 2—4 and Figure 7A, F–H) is the principal bone of the lateral surface of the jaw, and bears a single row of teeth.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and direct observation.

claims.claim: The prearticular of †Brachydegma occupies most of the mesial surface of the lower jaw.
claims.source: The prearticular occupies most of the mesial surface of the lower jaw, but no teeth are apparent in the tomograms.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: Coronoids cannot be distinguished from the prearticular in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: Coronoids cannot be distinguished from the prearticular.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: There is no well-developed coronoid process in †Brachydegma.
claims.source: There is no well-developed coronoid process, but a faint one at best formed by the surangular alone.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The deep adductor fossa of †Brachydegma is surrounded by the articular posteriorly, the prearticular medially, and the surangular and dentary laterally.
claims.source: The deep adductor fossa is surrounded by the articular posteriorly, the prearticular medially, and the surangular and dentary laterally.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: In addition to the two depressions for the quadrate, the articular of †Brachydegma bears a posterior flat facet for the insertion of the condyle of the symplectic.
claims.source: In addition to the two depressions for the quadrate, the articular bears a posterior flat facet for the insertion of the condyle of the symplectic (syf, Figure 7G, H).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The clavicles of †Brachydegma are broad triangular plates covering the anterior process of the massive cleithra.
claims.source: The clavicles are broad triangular plates covering the anterior process of the massive cleithra, resembling the primitive (Nielsen, 1942; Gardiner, 1984) condition associated with non-neopterygians (Jollie, 1984; Hilton et al., 2011) but retained in †parasemionotids (Olsen, 1984) and some stem teleosts (Arratia, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The cleithra of †Brachydegma lack the well-developed postbranchial lamina of many deeply diverging actinopterygians.
claims.source: The cleithra lack the well-developed postbranchial lamina of many deeply diverging actinopterygians like †Trawdenia (Coates and Tietjen, 2018), but also extant chondrosteans (Hilton et al., 2011) and the parasemionotid †Watsonulus (Olsen, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The cleithrum of †Brachydegma is rather tall and forms an acute dorsal tip.
claims.source: The cleithrum is rather tall and forms an acute dorsal tip.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The posterior notch of the cleithrum of †Brachydegma faces posteroventrally.
claims.source: The posterior notch of the cleithrum faces posteroventrally.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The dorsal (scapular) portion of the scapulocoracoid of †Brachydegma is well developed on both sides.
claims.source: The dorsal (scapular) portion of the scapulocoracoid is well developed on both sides, whereas the ventral (coracoid) portion is not preserved and was conceivably cartilaginous.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and inference about unossified structures.

claims.claim: The ventral (coracoid) portion of the scapulocoracoid of †Brachydegma is not preserved and was conceivably cartilaginous.
claims.source: The dorsal (scapular) portion of the scapulocoracoid is well developed on both sides, whereas the ventral (coracoid) portion is not preserved and was conceivably cartilaginous.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and inference about unossified structures.

claims.claim: The notochord of †Brachydegma is unconstricted, and only arcual elements are apparent.
claims.source: The notochord is unconstricted, and only arcual elements are apparent (arc, bd, bv, Figure 10H–J).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: Supraneurals are not observed in the anterior vertebral segments of †Brachydegma.
claims.source: Supraneurals are not observed in the anterior vertebral segments.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The rhomboid scales of †Brachydegma exhibit a dorsal articular peg and a small anterodorsal process.
claims.source: The rhomboid scales (Figure 10K) of †Brachydegma exhibit a dorsal articular peg and a small anterodorsal process.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The equally weighted parsimony analysis recovered 1412 most parsimonious trees of 1652 steps.
claims.source: Our equally weighted parsimony analysis recovered 1412 most parsimonious trees of 1652 steps (Figure 11).
claims.evidence: This is a result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The crown neopterygian clade receives low Bremer support in the equally weighted parsimony analysis.
claims.source: The crown neopterygian clade receives low Bremer support in our analysis (Bremer decay index [BDI]=2), and is diagnosed on the basis of eight synapomorphies, two of which are unique (marked here with *): anterior expansion of lachrymal (C.53); presence of multiple rami of infraorbital canal in jugal (C.56); mobile maxilla (C.73); presence of a peg-like anterior maxillary process (C.74*); presence of an interopercle (C.119*); internal carotid artery piercing the parasphenoid (C.180); presence of two ossifications of the ceratohyal (C.219); presence of ossified centra (C.287).
claims.evidence: This is a result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: †Brachydegma can be confidently excluded from the neopterygian crown.
claims.source: These are all absent in †Brachydegma, which furthermore lacks any form of coronoid process, an essential component of the crown neopterygian hallmark. Therefore, †Brachydegma can be confidently excluded from the neopterygian crown, contrary to previous hypotheses (Hurley et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis and anatomical observations.

claims.claim: In the parsimony strict consensus tree, †Brachydegma is resolved as sister to a clade containing †birgeriids and †scanilepiforms + polypterids.
claims.source: In our parsimony strict consensus tree (Figure 11), †Brachydegma is resolved as sister to a clade containing †birgeriids and †scanilepiforms + polypterids.
claims.evidence: This is a result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: When †Brachydegma is constrained with halecomorphs and †Watsonulus, the resulting MPTs are 13 steps longer than the unconstrained parsimony analyses.
claims.source: When †Brachydegma is constrained with halecomorphs and †Watsonulus (Hurley et al., 2007), the resulting MPTs are 13 steps longer (1665 vs. 1652 steps).
claims.evidence: This is a result of the constrained phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: When †Brachydegma is constrained in a monophyletic clade with actinopterans, the analyses resulted in MPTs that are three steps longer than the unconstrained parsimony analyses.
claims.source: When †Brachydegma is constrained in a monophyletic clade with actinopterans (Giles et al., 2017), the analyses resulted in MPTs that are three steps longer (1655 steps) than the unconstrained parsimony analyses.
claims.evidence: This is a result of the constrained phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: When reanalyzing the phylogenetic matrix after excluding †Brachydegma, the resolution of post-Devonian actinopterygian interrelationships is largely lost.
claims.source: When reanalyzing our phylogenetic matrix after excluding †Brachydegma, but keeping newly added/modified characters, clades recovered in the previous rounds of analyses are not resolved (1646 steps; Appendix 1—figure 4). Instead, the resolution of post-Devonian actinopterygian interrelationships is largely lost, and is replaced by a large polytomy containing major groups (e.g., †Scanilepiformes + Polypteridae, Chondrostei, and a poorly resolved neopterygian total group).
claims.evidence: This is a result of the phylogenetic analysis excluding †Brachydegma.

claims.claim: In the implied weights parsimony analysis, †Brachydegma is resolved as a stem neopterygian.
claims.source: In the strict consensus, †Brachydegma is resolved as a stem neopterygian, on the basis of three synapomorphies of varying fit scores (f): presence of a vertical preopercle (C.116; f:0.37); length of the median gular exceeding half the length of the lower jaw (C.124; f:0.14); and the presence of uncinate processes of the epibranchials (C.231; f:0.2).
claims.evidence: This is a result of the implied weights phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The exclusion of †Brachydegma from the neopterygian crown group is ratified in the Bayesian analysis.
claims.source: The exclusion of †Brachydegma from the neopterygian crown group is ratified in our Bayesian analysis (Appendix 1—figure 6), where the neopterygian crown is strongly supported (BPP=0.99).
claims.evidence: This is a result of the Bayesian phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: †Brachydegma is unique among described Permian actinopterygians in preserving the external dermal skeleton, braincase, hyoid arch, gill skeleton, and shoulder girdle in three dimensions.
claims.source: †Brachydegma is thus far unique among described Permian actinopterygians in preserving the external dermal skeleton, braincase, hyoid arch, gill skeleton, and shoulder girdle in three dimensions.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the preservation quality and completeness of †Brachydegma compared to other Permian taxa.

claims.claim: †Brachydegma represents an important addition between earlier Devonian-Carboniferous and later Triassic taxa for which detailed anatomical information is available.
claims.source: It therefore represents an important addition between earlier Devonian-Carboniferous (e.g., †Mimipiscis [Gardiner, 1984]; †Raynerius [Giles et al., 2015b]; †Lawrenciella [Poplin, 1974; Pradel et al., 2016]; †Trawdenia [Coates, 1999; Coates and Tietjen, 2018]; †Coccocephalichthys [Poplin and Véran, 1996]) and later Triassic taxa (e.g., †Watsonulus [Olsen, 1984]; †Saurichthys [Argyriou et al., 2018]; †'Perleidus' and early teleosts [Patterson, 1975]) for which similar detailed anatomical information is available.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the temporal and anatomical significance of †Brachydegma, supported by citations.

claims.claim: †Brachydegma bears a novel combination of traits.
claims.source: †Brachydegma bears a novel combination of traits, but this is unsurprising given how little is known of the internal anatomy of any other Permian actinopterygian (but see Gill, 1923; Aldinger, 1937).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the unique character combination in †Brachydegma, contextualized by the knowledge gap for Permian taxa.

claims.claim: The braincase and parasphenoid of †Brachydegma display an unexpected combination of features.
claims.source: The braincase and parasphenoid of †Brachydegma display an unexpected combination of features.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the anatomical findings.

claims.claim: †Brachydegma exhibits differentiated endochondral ossifications in the occipital region, which is the earliest example of a condition typically associated with neopterygians.
claims.source: Rather than having a single, co-ossified occipital arch, †Brachydegma exhibits differentiated endochondral ossifications in the occipital region. This is the earliest example of a condition typically associated with neopterygians (Patterson, 1975; Grande and Bemis, 1998; Grande, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with neopterygians, with temporal significance inferred.

claims.claim: The posterior parasphenoid stem extending behind the ventral otic fissure clearly differentiates †Brachydegma from most anatomically generalized Paleozoic-early Mesozoic actinopterygians.
claims.source: The posterior parasphenoid stem extending behind the ventral otic fissure clearly differentiates †Brachydegma from most anatomically generalized Paleozoic-early Mesozoic actinopterygians (Nielsen, 1942; Nielsen, 1949; Schaeffer and Dalquest, 1978; Gardiner, 1984; Giles et al., 2015b; Figueroa et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The bifurcation of the dorsal aorta into lateral dorsal aortae occurs below the posterior stem of the parasphenoid in †Brachydegma, resembling the condition seen in †saurichthyiforms, conceivably †birgeriids and most actinopterans, but not polypterids.
claims.source: The bifurcation of the dorsal aorta into lateral dorsal aortae occurs below the posterior stem of the parasphenoid in †Brachydegma, resembling the condition seen in †saurichthyiforms (Argyriou et al., 2018), conceivably †birgeriids (Nielsen, 1949) and most actinopterans (Patterson, 1975), but not polypterids (Allis, 1922).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The presence of a dorsolateral metapterygoideal flange and groove in †Brachydegma is a possibly derived feature.
claims.source: The presence of a dorsolateral metapterygoideal flange and groove in †Brachydegma is a possibly derived feature, which is encountered in a rudimentary form in †Australosomus (Nielsen, 1949), but is otherwise largely restricted to neopterygians (Olsen, 1984; Arratia and Schultze, 1991).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The intimate contact between the palate and the maxilla in †Brachydegma is reminiscent of the primitive configuration seen in most stem and early diverging actinopterygians, and to an extent in Polypterus.
claims.source: By contrast to the above, the intimate contact between the palate and the maxilla, via overlapping flanges issuing from the ventral surfaces of both bones, is reminiscent of the primitive configuration seen in most stem and early diverging actinopterygians, and to an extent in Polypterus (Nielsen, 1942; Nielsen, 1949; Gardiner, 1984; Giles et al., 2017; Argyriou et al., 2018; Lemberg et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The nearly complete branchial skeleton of †Brachydegma represents one of the best examples known so far from a Paleozoic-early Mesozoic actinopterygian.
claims.source: The nearly complete branchial skeleton of †Brachydegma represents one of the best examples known so far from a Paleozoic-early Mesozoic actinopterygian (Stensiö, 1921; Stensiö, 1932; Aldinger, 1937; Nielsen, 1942; Nielsen, 1949; Giles et al., 2015b; Giles et al., 2017; Argyriou et al., 2018; Figueroa et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the quality and completeness of the branchial skeleton, supported by citations.

claims.claim: †Brachydegma shares five gill arches with most Permian-Triassic actinopterygians, chondrosteans, and most teleosts.
claims.source: Unlike polypterids (Allis, 1922), †Brachydegma shares five gill arches – with the fifth represented only by a pair of tiny ceratobranchials – and four independent hypobranchial ossifications with most Permian-Triassic actinopterygians (Nielsen, 1942; Nielsen, 1949; Giles et al., 2017), chondrosteans (Grande and Bemis, 1991; Hilton et al., 2011), and most teleosts (Nelson, 1969; Hilton, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The dorsal gill skeleton of †Brachydegma lacks enlarged tooth patches.
claims.source: The dorsal gill skeleton of †Brachydegma lacks enlarged tooth patches and has a well-ossified series of suprapharyngobranchials; both contrast with derived conditions found in neopterygians (Nelson, 1969; Grande and Bemis, 1998; Hilton, 2002; Grande, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with neopterygians.

claims.claim: The dorsal gill skeleton of †Brachydegma has a well-ossified series of suprapharyngobranchials.
claims.source: The dorsal gill skeleton of †Brachydegma lacks enlarged tooth patches and has a well-ossified series of suprapharyngobranchials; both contrast with derived conditions found in neopterygians (Nelson, 1969; Grande and Bemis, 1998; Hilton, 2002; Grande, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with neopterygians.

claims.claim: Shoulder girdles and their patterns of variation remain poorly characterized in early fossil actinopterygians.
claims.source: Shoulder girdles and their patterns of variation remain poorly characterized in early fossil actinopterygians.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The dermal shoulder girdle of †Brachydegma differs from the reduced complement of dermal bones in neopterygians.
claims.source: The dermal shoulder girdle of †Brachydegma is well developed, comprising large supracleithra, presupracleithra, cleithra, postcleithra, and clavicles, differing from the reduced complement of dermal bones in neopterygians.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with neopterygians.

claims.claim: The endoskeletal girdle of †Brachydegma is only partially mineralized.
claims.source: However, the endoskeletal girdle is only partially mineralized, in contrast to those of most Devonian-Carboniferous taxa (Gardiner, 1984; Coates and Tietjen, 2018), but bearing some possible resemblance to the much-modified girdles of living actinopterygians (Jessen, 1972; Grande and Bemis, 1998; Grande, 2010; Hilton et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: †Brachydegma lacks a mineralized coracoid plate or completely mineralized mesocoracoid arch.
claims.source: †Brachydegma lacks a mineralized coracoid plate or completely mineralized mesocoracoid arch, in contrast to most deeply diverging actinopterygians (Nielsen, 1942; Jessen, 1972; Gardiner, 1984; Coates and Tietjen, 2018) and the Triassic neopterygian †Watsonulus (Olsen, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The lack of a dorsal scapular process in †Brachydegma resembles stem actinopterygians such as †Trawdenia.
claims.source: The lack of a dorsal scapular process resembles stem actinopterygians such as †Trawdenia (Coates and Tietjen, 2018), and clearly differs from the earliest neopterygian pectoral girdle known, that of †Watsonulus (Olsen, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The hyoid arch of †Brachydegma shows the presence of two accessory hyoid elements between the dorsal and ventral components of the arch.
claims.source: Perhaps most surprisingly, the hyoid arch of †Brachydegma shows the presence of two accessory hyoid elements between the dorsal and ventral components of the arch.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The two accessory hyoid ossifications of †Brachydegma exhibit a sub-parallel arrangement.
claims.source: These two ossifications exhibit a sub-parallel arrangement, with the anteriormost articulating with the lower jaw to form a double jaw joint.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The anteriormost accessory hyoid ossification of †Brachydegma articulates with the lower jaw to form a double jaw joint.
claims.source: These two ossifications exhibit a sub-parallel arrangement, with the anteriormost articulating with the lower jaw to form a double jaw joint.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data.

claims.claim: The unanticipated combination of characters found in †Brachydegma is associated with ambiguity in its phylogenetic position.
claims.source: The unanticipated combination of characters found in †Brachydegma is associated with ambiguity in its phylogenetic position, with equal weights parsimony, implied weights parsimony, and Bayesian analyses yielding conflicting placements.
claims.evidence: This is based on the results of multiple phylogenetic analyses.

claims.claim: The volatility of early actinopterygian phylogeny between successive studies suggests that these hypotheses should be viewed with caution.
claims.source: The volatility of early actinopterygian phylogeny between successive studies using similar character sets but different taxon samples suggests that these hypotheses should be viewed with caution, until more information of both the internal and external anatomy of additional late Paleozoic-early Mesozoic fossil groups becomes available (Giles et al., 2017; Argyriou et al., 2018; Latimer and Giles, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of conflicting phylogenetic results across studies.

claims.claim: The reappraisal of the systematic affinities of †Brachydegma contrasts sharply with past hypotheses of crown neopterygian affinity.
claims.source: Our reappraisal of the systematic affinities of †Brachydegma contrasts sharply with past hypotheses of crown neopterygian affinity (Hurley et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analyses and anatomical observations.

claims.claim: Evidence previously advanced for a neopterygian placement of †Brachydegma included the presence of a supraorbital bone, a large median gular, a posteriorly indented and possibly free maxilla, an antorbital with a tube-like anterior process, and a neopterygian-like coronoid process.
claims.source: Evidence previously advanced for a neopterygian (and specifically halecomorph) placement of †Brachydegma included the presence of: a supraorbital bone; a large median gular; a posteriorly indented and possibly free maxilla; an antorbital with a tube-like anterior process; and a neopterygian-like coronoid process (Hurley et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of previous arguments, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The majority of characters previously used to support neopterygian affinity of †Brachydegma are either widely distributed across actinopterygians or were misidentified.
claims.source: The majority of these characters are either widely distributed across actinopterygians (supraorbitals, antorbital with a tube-like anterior process) or were misidentified in †Brachydegma (posteriorly indented maxilla, free maxilla, coronoid process, and the possible misidentification of the nasal as an antorbital).
claims.evidence: This is based on the new anatomical observations and comparisons.

claims.claim: The homology and evolution of hyoid elements is complex.
claims.source: The homology and evolution of hyoid elements is complex, and our new data on the hyoid arch of †Brachydegma add to this long-running debate (Patterson, 1973; Jollie, 1980; Patterson, 1982; Jollie, 1984; Véran, 1988; Gardiner and Schaeffer, 1989; Gardiner et al., 2005; Warth et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Polypterids possess a single accessory hyoid element that articulates with the full width of the hyomandibula dorsally and of the ceratohyal ventrally.
claims.source: Polypterids possess a single accessory hyoid element that articulates with the full width of the hyomandibula dorsally and of the ceratohyal ventrally (Allis, 1922; Moy-thomas, 1933; Jollie, 1984; Giles et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about polypterids, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The single accessory hyoid element in polypterids develops independently of the hyosymplectic cartilage and thus represents an interhyal.
claims.source: This bone develops independently of the hyosymplectic cartilage and thus represents an interhyal (Moy-thomas, 1933; Jollie, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is based on developmental studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Neopterygians primitively have two accessory elements between the hyomandibula and ceratohyal.
claims.source: Neopterygians primitively have two accessory elements between the hyomandibula and ceratohyal.
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about neopterygians.

claims.claim: The symplectic in neopterygians typically braces the mandibular arch.
claims.source: The more anterior of these – the symplectic – typically braces the mandibular arch (Patterson, 1973; Olsen, 1984; Véran, 1988; Gardiner and Schaeffer, 1989; Gardiner et al., 1996; Grande and Bemis, 1998; Grande, 2010; Arratia, 2013) and arises as an anteroventral outgrowth of the embryonic hyosymplectic cartilage that subsequently detaches in development (Holmgren, 1943; Bertmar, 1959; Konstantinidis et al., 2015; Mork and Crump, 2015; DeLaurier, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical and developmental knowledge about neopterygians, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The symplectic in neopterygians arises as an anteroventral outgrowth of the embryonic hyosymplectic cartilage that subsequently detaches in development.
claims.source: The more anterior of these – the symplectic – typically braces the mandibular arch (Patterson, 1973; Olsen, 1984; Véran, 1988; Gardiner and Schaeffer, 1989; Gardiner et al., 1996; Grande and Bemis, 1998; Grande, 2010; Arratia, 2013) and arises as an anteroventral outgrowth of the embryonic hyosymplectic cartilage that subsequently detaches in development (Holmgren, 1943; Bertmar, 1959; Konstantinidis et al., 2015; Mork and Crump, 2015; DeLaurier, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on developmental studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The interhyal in neopterygians articulates with the posteroventral portion of the hyomandibula and suspends the ventral hyoid elements.
claims.source: The more posterior accessory element – the interhyal – articulates with the posteroventral portion of the hyomandibula and suspends the ventral hyoid elements (Patterson, 1982; Véran, 1988; Grande and Bemis, 1998; Grande, 2010; Konstantinidis et al., 2015; DeLaurier, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about neopterygians, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The interhyal in neopterygians arises from an independent embryonic cartilage.
claims.source: The interhyal arises from an independent embryonic cartilage (Konstantinidis et al., 2015; Mork and Crump, 2015; DeLaurier, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on developmental studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The interhyal remains cartilaginous in adult holosteans.
claims.source: The interhyal remains cartilaginous in adult holosteans (Grande and Bemis, 1998; Grande, 2010), while the symplectic shows contrasting conditions in different members of that group.
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about holosteans, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In halecomorphs, the symplectic is hatchet shaped and articulates with the articular forming a second jaw joint.
claims.source: In halecomorphs, it is hatchet shaped and articulates with the articular forming a second jaw joint (Grande and Bemis, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about halecomorphs, supported by citation.

claims.claim: In ginglymodans, the symplectic is 'L' shaped and joins the back of the primary palate.
claims.source: In ginglymodans, it is 'L' shaped and joins the back of the primary palate (Grande, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about ginglymodans, supported by citation.

claims.claim: In extant teleosts, the symplectic is wedge-shaped and typically inserts in a notch on the quadrate.
claims.source: In extant teleosts, the symplectic is wedge-shaped and typically inserts in a notch on the quadrate, while the interhyal is variably ossified and lies between the hyomandibula and posterior ceratohyal (Hilton, 2002; Arratia, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about teleosts, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Both the number and identity of accessory hyoid elements in acipenseriforms has been the subject of considerable debate.
claims.source: In contrast to the uncontroversial assessments for polypterids and neopterygians, both the number and identity of accessory hyoid elements in acipenseriforms has been the subject of considerable debate.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge and debate in the field.

claims.claim: Traquair, 1877 proposed that there are two accessory hyoid elements in acipenseriforms: the dorsal one representing a symplectic, and the ventral one representing an interhyal.
claims.source: The first, initially proposed by Traquair, 1877 and adopted by several subsequent authors (Sewertzoff, 1928; Marinelli and Strenger, 1973; Jollie, 1980; Véran, 1988), is that there are two accessory hyoid elements: the dorsal one representing a symplectic, and the ventral one representing an interhyal.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a hypothesis proposed by Traquair, 1877 and supported by other authors.

claims.claim: Patterson, 1982 posits that the dorsal bone or cartilage in acipenseriforms is an interhyal.
claims.source: The second, most forcefully argued by Patterson, 1982, posits that the dorsal bone or cartilage is an interhyal.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a hypothesis proposed by Patterson, 1982.

claims.claim: Patterson's (1982) model for acipenseriform hyoid elements is now dominant.
claims.source: Patterson's (1982) model is now dominant (e.g., Gardiner, 1984; Gardiner and Schaeffer, 1989; Gardiner et al., 1996; Coates, 1999; Gardiner et al., 2005; Grande, 2010; Xu et al., 2014; Warth et al., 2017; López-Arbarello and Sferco, 2018; Xu, 2019), but neither scheme is without its challenges.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current consensus in the field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: †Brachydegma provides a new perspective on the debate about hyoid element homology.
claims.source: †Brachydegma provides a new perspective on this debate (Figures 8 and 12) for two reasons. First, it preserves two accessory hyoid elements in three dimensions and life position. Second, its phylogenetic position, although ambiguous, clearly lies far outside halecomorphs, or the neopterygian crown.
claims.evidence: This is based on the anatomical observations and phylogenetic position of †Brachydegma.

claims.claim: The more anterior element of †Brachydegma matches structural criteria used to identify the symplectic in crown neopterygians.
claims.source: In this context, it is significant that the more anterior element matches structural criteria used to identify the symplectic in crown neopterygians: it lies immediately posterior to the quadrate, between the hyomandibula and lower jaw, and it forms a clear articulation with the latter via a condyle (Patterson, 1973; Patterson, 1982; Gardiner et al., 1996; Grande and Bemis, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical observations and comparison with neopterygians.

claims.claim: A further similarity between the anterior element of †Brachydegma and the undisputed symplectic of †parasemionotids is the presence of an aortic groove.
claims.source: A further similarity between this anterior element of †Brachydegma and the undisputed symplectic of †parasemionotids is the presence of an aortic groove (sensu Véran, 1988) on the dorsal anterolateral and lateral surface of the bone (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical observations and comparison with †parasemionotids.

claims.claim: Under the interpretation that the anterior element of †Brachydegma is a symplectic, the slender, rod-shaped posterior element would represent an interhyal.
claims.source: Under this interpretation, the slender, rod-shaped posterior element of †Brachydegma would represent an interhyal.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the identification of the anterior element as a symplectic.

claims.claim: μCT-aided examination of the hyoid arch of †Pteronisculus gunnari revealed a single accessory element.
claims.source: Our μCT-aided examination of the hyoid arch of the putative stem actinopterygian †Pteronisculus gunnari revealed a single accessory element (Figure 8J–M), which presents many similarities with the symplectic of †Brachydegma and also satisfies most criteria for establishing its homology with the neopterygian symplectic.
claims.evidence: This is based on CT data from †Pteronisculus.

claims.claim: The single accessory element of †Pteronisculus presents many similarities with the symplectic of †Brachydegma.

results.result: CT scanning of †Brachydegma reveals a unique mosaic of primitive and derived anatomical features. The fossil exhibits primitive features including an aortic canal and immobile maxilla, alongside derived features such as differentiated occipital ossifications, posterior parasphenoid stem, two accessory hyoid ossifications arranged sub-parallel, and a double jaw joint. The braincase, palate, branchial skeleton, shoulder girdle, and hyoid arch are described in unprecedented detail for a Permian actinopterygian.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C196 collectively document detailed anatomical observations from CT data (Figures 2-10), providing comprehensive descriptions of external and internal skeletal anatomy. The observations are internally consistent, well-illustrated, and represent direct data from high-quality 3D preservation. The anatomical descriptions form the empirical foundation for subsequent phylogenetic and evolutionary interpretations.

results.result: Phylogenetic analyses using multiple methods (equal weights parsimony, implied weights parsimony, Bayesian) yield conflicting placements for †Brachydegma, either on the polypterid stem or as an early-diverging stem neopterygian. However, all analyses decisively reject previous placement within the neopterygian crown. The taxon lacks key crown neopterygian synapomorphies including mobile maxilla, peg-like anterior maxillary process, interopercle, and coronoid process.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C199 document phylogenetic results showing consistent exclusion of †Brachydegma from crown Neopterygii across all analytical methods (C167-C175), despite ambiguity in its precise position. Constrained analyses requiring 13 additional steps for halecomorph placement (C171) and strong Bayesian support (BPP=0.99) for crown Neopterygii excluding †Brachydegma (C175) provide robust statistical support. The anatomical basis for exclusion is clearly documented (C168-C169).

results.result: †Brachydegma preserves two accessory hyoid elements in three dimensions: an anterior symplectic and posterior interhyal arranged sub-parallel, with the symplectic forming a double jaw joint with the articular. The symplectic identification is supported by position, morphology, articulation with the lower jaw via a condyle, and presence of an aortic groove. Similar features are identified in †Pteronisculus and confirmed in †Boreosomus, suggesting widespread distribution of symplectic in stem actinopterygians.
results.evaluation: Claims C194-C230 present anatomical evidence (C194-C196, C219-C220) supported by CT data (Figure 8) and comparative analysis with †parasemionotids, †Pteronisculus (C222-C224), and direct observation of †Boreosomus specimens (C227). The identification criteria are explicit and consistent with neopterygian symplectic morphology (C219). The inference about widespread distribution (C226, C230) is supported by multiple lines of comparative evidence, though developmental data are unavailable for fossils.

results.result: Key endoskeletal components of the hyoid suspensorium previously thought restricted to crown neopterygians (symplectic, interhyal arrangement, double jaw joint) appeared deeper in actinopterygian phylogeny than previously recognized. The double jaw joint can no longer be treated as a unique halecomorph synapomorphy, and convergent evolution of these features becomes unlikely given their presence in stem actinopterygians.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C15, C218, C229-C230 represent major evolutionary inferences directly supported by the anatomical observations (Result 3) and phylogenetic placement (Result 2) of †Brachydegma. The logic is sound: if †Brachydegma possesses these features and lies outside crown Neopterygii, then these features evolved earlier than previously thought. The argument against convergence (C230) is strengthened by evidence from multiple stem taxa (C225-C227).

results.result: The manuscript establishes context for †Brachydegma within actinopterygian evolution, documenting its temporal placement (early Permian), preservation quality, previous phylogenetic interpretations, and the importance of hyoid arch anatomy for understanding actinopterygian relationships. The Permian represents a major knowledge gap for actinopterygian biology, and †Brachydegma is one of few Permian taxa with three-dimensional cranial preservation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C58 provide background knowledge and context, supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These establish the significance of †Brachydegma (C47-C48), document conflicting prior interpretations (C4, C51-C57), and review established knowledge about actinopterygian diversity (C16-C20), divergence timing (C21-C22), and hyoid arch variation (C30-C43). The knowledge gap for Permian taxa (C46) and importance of endoskeletal characters (C23-C24) justify the study's focus.

results.result: Both †Brachydegma specimens are from the stratigraphically oldest deposits of the Clear Fork Formation, Baylor County, Texas, biostratigraphically dated to the late Kungurian-early Roadian interval (late Cisuralian, ~283.5-266.9 Ma). The formation represents coastal floodplain environments with accompanying vertebrate fauna including †xenacanths, lungfishes, and †Dimetrodon.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 document geological context supported by citations to Nelson et al. 2013 and other geological literature. The stratigraphic and temporal placement is clearly established, providing essential context for the fossil's age and depositional environment. This information is factual and well-supported by cited sources.

results.result: Previous evidence for neopterygian affinity of †Brachydegma (supraorbital bone, large median gular, posteriorly indented maxilla, antorbital, coronoid process) is reinterpreted. Most characters are either widely distributed across actinopterygians or were misidentified in †Brachydegma based on external examination alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C201 critically evaluate prior work (Hurley et al. 2007) based on new CT data. The reinterpretation is supported by detailed anatomical observations (e.g., C149 showing no posterior maxillary notch, C155 showing no well-developed coronoid process). This demonstrates how CT scanning reveals features not visible externally, correcting previous misinterpretations. The evaluation is fair and evidence-based.

results.result: The manuscript reviews established knowledge about hyoid element homology and evolution across actinopterygians. Polypterids have one interhyal; neopterygians primitively have symplectic and interhyal; acipenseriforms show debated interpretations (Traquair 1877 vs. Patterson 1982 models). The homology and evolution of these elements is complex and debated.
results.evaluation: Claims C202-C217 synthesize prior knowledge about hyoid arch anatomy and homology debates, extensively supported by citations. This review establishes the framework for interpreting †Brachydegma's hyoid anatomy. The presentation is balanced, acknowledging competing hypotheses (C215-C217) and their challenges. This contextualizes the significance of the new †Brachydegma data.
